content.content:
Label Buster is a step-by-step guide to help you identify the information you need to create a food label that meets Australian requirements. At the end of Label Buster, you will generate:

  • a product sheet you can give to a printer to design a label for you
  • an example of what your food label should look like.

The Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code (the Food Standards Code) sets the standards for food labelling in Australia. Significant penalties apply in Queensland under the Food Act 2006 (the Act), for non-compliance with the Food Standards Code.

content.heading: Did you know
content.content: Labels must have the same information whether you sell your product once at a market stall, or regularly to a supermarket.
Who can use Label Buster?

Label Buster is designed for small to medium food businesses. If your food has complex labelling requirements, such as infant formula, sports supplements or alcohol, the tool does not provide all the information you need, and you are recommended to seek professional legal advice from a food labelling consultant.

content.heading: Before you start
content.content:
To use Label Buster, you will need:

Up to 1 hour - if you are familiar with food labelling requirements.

Up to 2 hours - if you have never made a food label before.

You will need information about your food, such as:

  • ingredients
  • use-by or best-before dates
  • any storage conditions or directions for use

The questions marked with a * must be completed. Other questions are optional.

PLEASE NOTE: The Label Buster tool is in the process of being updated to incorporate the Plain English Allergen Labelling (PEAL) provisions of the Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code that came into effect on 25 February 2024.

IMPORTANT: After you have completed Label Buster, you will need to refer to the Allergen labelling fact sheet to make the required PEAL changes to your draft food label and ensure you have a label that is compliant with the Food Standards Code.
If your food contains any allergens, this will mainly involve changing the format of the ingredient list and including an allergy ‘summary statement’. It should only take an additional 5-10 minutes.
Another resource you may find helpful is Allergen labelling for food businesses, which is available on the Food Standards Australia New Zealand website.

If you have trouble or have any further questions in relation to incorporating the allergen requirements into your label, please contact the Food Safety Standards and Regulation Unit via foodsafety@health.qld.gov.au or phone (07) 3328 9310.

content.heading: Did you know
content.content: Label Buster will provide you with food labelling information to help you to comply with the Food Standards Code. After you finish Label Buster, you will need to include other mandatory requirements for a Nutrition Information Panel , weights and measures , and Country of origin labelling. Health Star Rating is a voluntary scheme you can choose to add to your food.
Please read and accept the terms of use before using Label Buster.

• Terms and conditions
  • Privacy statement
  • Disclaimer
  • Copyright

content.heading: Warning
content.content: Label Buster does not replace information provided by Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) about labelling requirements. Any reference you make to the Food Standards Code does not relieve you of your responsibility to review all current legislative requirements that apply to your business.
Your privacy is important to us. Please refer to the Queensland Government's privacy statement.

All the labelling requirements in this tool are current for packaged food labelling requirements. These requirements can be found in Part 1.2 - Labelling and Other Information Requirements of the Food Standards Code. The labelling requirements provided from this tool do not include:

  • nutrition information panel requirements (Standard 1.2.8)
  • legibility requirements (Standard 1.2.9)
  • percentage labelling requirements (Standard 1.2.10)
  • country of origin requirements (Standard 1.2.11).
This tool does not provide requirements for unpackaged foods. Contact the Food Safety Standards and Regulation Unit for information on unpackaged food labelling requirements.

This tool only provides summary information in relation to allergen labelling. For detailed information you should refer to Allergen labelling for food businesses on the FSANZ website and the Queensland Health Allergen labelling fact sheet.

content.content: Select on the food label sections below to learn about labels.

content.alt: An example label for strawberry yoghurt

items.title: 1. Food name and description
items.content:
Food labels must show the name of the food to help identify the food.

The name and description of the food must reflect its true nature. For example, strawberry yoghurt must contain strawberries. If the yoghurt contained strawberry flavouring rather than real fruit, then the name would need to indicate that it is strawberry-flavoured yoghurt.

If the name of the food does not reflect its true nature, then you must include a description of the true nature on the label. For example, Luke’s Hot’s Sauce (red chilli pepper sauce).

items.title: 2. Business details
items.content:
To help customers identify where food has come from or to use for a food recall when food is unsafe, a food label must include the following business details:

  • name of the business supplying the food
  • business address in Australia or New Zealand, or a description of the location, of the premises where the business is being operated. A postal address cannot be used.

items.title: 3. Weights
items.content:
The National Measurement Institute is responsible for making sure food is measured and weighed correctly, and that the food is labelled with the correct weight and unit.

For example, food labelled as being 500g should weigh 500g and use the metric system of grams (g), kilograms (kg), millilitres (mL), litres (L), etc.

Visit the NMI website for more information on how to comply with the laws around weights and other measures.

items.title: 4. Date marks
items.content:
Food packaged with a shelf life of 2 years or less must show a date mark.

Foods that should be eaten before a certain date for health and safety reasons must be labelled with a use-by date. Otherwise, a best-before date is required if the food has a shelf life of less than 2 years. Although it may be safe to eat the food after the best-before date, the food may have lost quality or some nutritional value.

Bread with a shelf-life of less than 7 days, can use a baked-for date or baked-on date instead of a best-before date.

items.title: 5. Lot identification
items.content: The lot identification means a number or other information that identifies where the food was made and the batch it was part of. It is not always necessary to include a lot identification on a label if a date mark, business name and address can identify the food. If date marking is not required, lot identification must be added so that the food can be identified.

items.title: 6. Storage conditions and directions for use
items.content:
Storage conditions
To keep food until its best-before or use-by date include storage conditions on your label.

Directions for use
A food label must have directions on how to use or prepare the food if needed for health and safety reasons.

items.title: 7. Ingredients
items.content: A food label must contain a list of ingredients. The Food Standards Code has rules that describe how each ingredient must be listed, how it is named, extra requirements if an ingredient contains allergens, and how the list is formatted.

items.title: 8. Advisory statements, warning statements and declarations
items.content: To help consumers avoid foods that are not safe for them to eat due to health conditions they may have, the Food Standards Code lists mandatory advisory statements, warning statements and allergen declarations that must be shown on a food label depending on the type of food and its ingredients.

items.title: 9. Nutrition information panel
items.content:
The nutrition information panel (NIP) shows the number of servings in the package and the average amounts in a serving of food and per 100 grams (or 100 millilitres) of food for:

  • energy (in kilojoules)
  • protein
  • fat (including saturated fat)
  • carbohydrates (including sugars)
  • sodium

If a nutrition, health or related claim is made, the NIP must also show the amount of nutrient or substance. For example: the amount of calcium must be shown in the nutrition information panel if a claim about calcium is made.

items.title: 10. Claims
items.content:
There are strict requirements about claims that can be made and how they should be written on a label.

Nutrition content claims are claims about the content of certain nutrients or substances in a food. For example, contains calcium.

Health claims refer to a relationship between food and health. For example, calcium for bone and teeth.

sections.title: Alcoholic drinks
sections.content:
Alcohol includes beer, wine and spirits and has unique and additional requirements such as number of standard drinks.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 2.7.1 Labelling of alcoholic beverages and food containing alcohol
  • Standard 2.7.2 Beer
  • Standard 2.7.3 Fruit wine, vegetable wine and mead
  • Standard 2.7.4 Wine and wine product
  • Standard 2.7.5 Spirits
  • Labelling of alcoholic beverages

sections.title: Claims: Nutrition, health and related claims
sections.content:
Nutrition, health and related claims are voluntary statements made by food businesses on labels and in advertising about the content of certain nutrients or substances in a food, or the relationship between food and health.

Claims cannot be made about:

  • kava
  • infant formula
  • any food that contains more than 1.15% alcohol by volume, other than a nutrition content claim about energy, carbohydrate or gluten content; or salt or sodium content about a food that is not a beverage.

Health claims

Health claims refer to a relationship between a food and health. For example:

  • Calcium for bones and teeth
  • Diets high in calcium may reduce the risk of osteoporosis in people 65 years and over

Health claims are not permitted on foods that are high in saturated fat, sugar or salt.
There are lists of pre-approved food-health relationships that businesses can base their claims on. These are listed in Schedule 4 of the Code.

Nutrition content claims

Nutrition content claims indicate the presence or absence of certain nutrients or substances in the food, for example, ‘low in fat’ or ‘good source of calcium’. These claims will need to meet certain criteria set out in the Standard. For example, food with a ‘good source of calcium’ claim will need to contain not less than the amount of calcium specified in the Standard.

Endorsements

An endorsement is a nutrition content claim or health claim that is made with the permission of an endorsing body, for example the Heart Foundation Tick.

Consumer value claims

Other consumer value claims such as cage free; organic or locally grown are covered by Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.7 Nutrition, health and related claims.
    • See section 1.2.7—23 Endorsing bodies
    • See section 1.2.7—24 Criteria for endorsements
  • Schedule 4 Nutrition, health and related claims
  • Australian Government Department of Health
    • Getting Your Claims Right 7. Endorsing bodies and endorsements https://www1.health.gov.au/internet/publications/publishing.nsf/Content/frs-getting-your-claims-right-toc~7-endorsing
  • Australian Competition and Consumer Commission
    • website https://www.accc.gov.au/business
    • Food and beverage industry – Food descriptors guideline to the Trade Practices Act

sections.title: Drinks made from cereals, nuts, and/or seeds
sections.content:
Drinks made from cereals, nuts and or seeds are not suitable for certain age groups, depending on the amount of protein and fats in the product. There are strict rules on how this information must be labelled.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

sections.title: Electrolyte drinks
sections.content:
Electrolyte drinks are formulated drinks which are designed for the rapid replacement of fluid, carbohydrates, electrolytes and minerals. These types of drinks, or drink bases, have strict rules about what substances are allowed and how this information must be labelled.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 2.6.2 Non-alcoholic beverages and brewed soft drinks

sections.title: Formulated caffeinated drinks
sections.content:
Formulated caffeinated drinks have very specific rules about what substances are allowed and how this information must be labelled.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 2.6.4 Formulated caffeinated beverages

sections.title: Genetically modified food
sections.content:
Food produced using gene technology means a food that has been derived or developed from an organism that has been genetically modified. Genetically modified food means a food produced using gene technology that contains novel DNA, novel protein or is listed in Schedule 26 of the Food Standard Code.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.5.2 Food produced using gene technology
  • Schedule 26 Food produced using gene technology

sections.title: Irradiated food
sections.content:
Food irradiation is a technology that improves the safety and extends the shelf life of foods by reducing or eliminating microorganisms and insects. Some fruits, vegetables, herbs and spices are allowed to be irradiated under strict conditions.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.5.3 Irradiation of food

sections.title: Novel foods
sections.content:
Novel foods are non-traditional foods that require a safety assessment by FSANZ before they used in Australia. Examples of novel foods include:

  • Dried marine micro-algae (Schizochytrium sp.) rich in docosahexaenoic acid
  • Insects for human consumption as a protein source

The Australian Novel Food Committee has developed resources to help determine if a food is a novel food that needs assessment.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.5.1 Novel foods
  • Schedule 25 Permitted Novel foods

sections.title: Special purpose foods
sections.content:
Special purpose foods have complex labelling requirements, such as an expanded nutrition information panel, compositional requirements and advisory statements. Special purpose foods include:

  • Infant formula products
  • Foods for infants
  • Formulated meal replacements and formulated supplementary foods
  • Formulated supplementary sports foods
  • Food for special medical purposes

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 2.9.1 Infant formula products
  • Standard 2.9.2 Food for infants
  • Standard 2.9.3 Formulated meal replacements and formulated supplementary foods
  • Standard 2.9.4 Formulated supplementary sports foods
  • Standard 2.9.5 Food for special medical purposes

sections.title: Required names
sections.content:
Special purpose foods have complex labelling requirements, such as an expanded nutrition information panel, compositional requirements and advisory statements. Special purpose foods include:

  • Infant formula products
  • Foods for infants
  • Formulated meal replacements and formulated supplementary foods
  • Formulated supplementary sports foods
  • Food for special medical purposes

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 2.9.1 Infant formula products
  • Standard 2.9.2 Food for infants
  • Standard 2.9.3 Formulated meal replacements and formulated supplementary foods
  • Standard 2.9.4 Formulated supplementary sports foods
  • Standard 2.9.5 Food for special medical purposes

content.description:
The purpose of a food name and description is to correctly describe what the food is. It cannot mislead the customer.

The Food Standards Code has rules on what you can name your food.

label.heading: Does your food name, or label, highlight an ingredient?
list: A picture of a honey pot on a muesli bar

content.heading: Characterising ingredients
content.content: Ingredients which are mentioned in the food name are called characterising ingredients. The Food Standards Code requires the amount of characterising ingredients to be shown in the ingredients list.

label.heading: Is your food one of the following:

content.heading: Prescribed names
content.content: These foods have names that must be used (prescribed names).

content.heading: Food with extra requirements
content.content:
Some foods have extra requirements. Use the Help guide to find out what they are.

For example: Ice cream must be made from milk to call it ice cream. Jam must be made from fruit to call it jam.

questions.label: Food name
questions.errorMessage: The food name must have 100 characters or less.

questions.label: Description
questions.errorMessage: The food description must have 250 characters or less.

sections.title: About food names
sections.content:
Food names must correctly describe the food. For example, strawberry yoghurt must contain strawberries. If the yoghurt contains strawberry flavouring instead of the fruit, then the name would need to be strawberry-flavoured yoghurt.

The Food Standards Code includes definitions for many foods, which includes what a food is made of. For example, a fruit juice cannot contain added water but a fruit drink can have water added.

Some food have names that must be used (prescribed names). For example, ‘fermented processed meat – cooked’ or ‘infant formula’.

The name of the food must not include words, statements, claims, pictures or graphics that represent a food in a way that is untrue, misleading or dishonest. For example, you cannot show a picture of honey on a yoghurt that does not contain honey.

If the name of the food does not reflect its true nature, then you must include a description of the true nature on the label. For example, Luke’s Hot’s Sauce (red chilli pepper sauce).

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.1.1 Structure of the Code and general provisions
    • See section 1.1.1—13 for food sold with a specified name or representation

sections.title: Characterising ingredients
sections.content:
A characterising ingredient or component of a food is:

  • mentioned in the name of the food; or
  • usually associated with name of the food by a consumer; or
  • emphasised on the label of the food in words or pictures.

If an ingredient is usually associated with the food (for example, fruit in Christmas pudding), or is highlighted on the label in words, pictures, or graphics, then it is a characterising ingredient. For example:

  • Strawberries are a characterising ingredient in strawberry yogurt
  • Meat is a characterising ingredient in a meat pie
  • Honey is a characterising ingredient where a yoghurt label shows a picture of a pot of honey

The amount of the characterising ingredients in the food must be written on the label as a percentage or, if declared in the nutrition information panel, as the average quantity per serving and per unit quantity.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.10 Information requirements – characterising ingredients and components of food.

Food Standards Australia New Zealand

  • User Guide – Percentage labelling of food

sections.title: Prescribed names
sections.content:
The following are considered prescribed names under the Food Standards Code and must be used when naming these foods.

  • fermented manufactured meat – cooked
  • fermented manufactured meat – heat treated
  • fermented manufactured meat – not heat treated
  • fermented processed meat – cooked
  • fermented processed meat – heat treated
  • fermented processed meat – not heat treated
  • honey

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.2.1 Meat and meat products
  • Standard 2.8.2 Honey

sections.title: Breads, cereals and grains
sections.content:
There are rules for the use of wholegrain and wholemeal in the food name.

The names 'shortbread', 'crispbread' and 'unleavened bread' can be used for foods which are not 'bread', because a consumer understands that they are not 'bread' as defined in the Food Standards Code.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.1.1 —13 Food sold with a specified name or representation
  • Standard 2.1.1

sections.title: Chocolate and cocoa
sections.content:
When naming a food chocolate, it must be:

  • made from cocoa bean products; and
  • have no more than 50 g/kg of edible oils (other than cocoa butter or dairy fats); and
  • be prepared from a minimum of 200 g/kg of cocoa bean products.

When naming a food cocoa, it must be made from cocoa beans, from which a portion of the fat can have been removed. Cocoa can contain added salt or spices.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.10.4 Miscellaneous standards for other foods

sections.title: Food containing alcohol
sections.content:
A food containing alcohol must not be represented in a way that suggests the food is non-alcoholic.

For example:

  • Rum balls
  • Brandy custard
  • Vanilla bean paste

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.7.1 Labelling of alcoholic beverages and food containing alcohol

sections.title: Fruit and vegetables
sections.content:
If the food is drink made from fruit or vegetables: There are naming rules for juice, juice blends and juice drinks. Please read the Food Standards Code to determine which one applies to your food.

If the food is a jam: If you name a food jam, it must be made from no less than 400 g/kg of fruit.

A jam can include conserve but it does not include marmalade.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.3.2 Jam
  • Standard 2.6.1 Fruit juice and vegetable juice

sections.title: Hemp food products
sections.content:
If the food is, or contains, allowed low THC hemp: The label must not include the words 'cannabis', 'marijuana' or similar. The label cannot have pictures of any part of a cannabis plant other than the seed.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.4.4 Prohibited and restricted plants and fungi

sections.title: Honey and honey products
sections.content:
Honey means the natural sweet substance produced by honey bees.

Food that is labelled as 'honey' must:

  • be honey; and
  • contain no less than 60% reducing sugars; and no more than 21% moisture.

The food name and description must contain the prescribed name of 'honey'.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.2 Information requirements – food identification
  • Standard 2.8.2 Honey

sections.title: Jams
sections.content:
If you name a food jam, it must be made from no less than 400 g/kg of fruit.

A jam can include conserve, but does not include marmalade

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.3.2 Jam

sections.title: Kava and kava root
sections.content:
Kava and kava root are allowed to be sold in Australia only if the food is:

  • A drink made from kava root using cold water; or
  • Dried or raw kava root.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.6.3 Kava

sections.title: Meat and meat products
sections.content:
There are naming rules for meat, including jerky, meat pies and sausages.

There are prescribed names for fermented manufactured meat.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.2.1 Meat and meat products

sections.title: Milk, dairy and dairy alternatives
sections.content:
If your food is milk, dairy or dairy alternative, you need to read the Food Standards Code to identify the necessary naming format. For example, the ingredient name 'soy' in soy milk or soy ice cream indicates that these foods are not dairy products.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.1.1 Structure of the code and general provisions
    • See section 1.1.1—13 for food sold with a specified name or representation
  • Standard 2.5.1 Milk
  • Standard 2.5.2 Cream
  • Standard 2.5.3 Fermented milk products
  • Standard 2.5.4 Cheese
  • Standard 2.5.5 Butter
  • Standard 2.5.6 Ice cream
  • Standard 2.5.7 Dried milk, evaporated milk and condensed milk

sections.title: Non-alcoholic drinks
sections.content:
If the food is drink made from fruit or vegetables: There are naming rules for juice, juice blends and juice drinks. Please read the Food Standards Code to determine which one applies to your food.

If the food is non-alcoholic or brewed soft drink: Non-alcoholic drinks and brewed soft drinks (e.g.: fermented ginger beer or kombucha) must not suggest the product is an alcoholic beverage. There is a possible risk that brewed soft drinks may contain alcohol which need extra labelling requirements. We recommend you seek professional advice to prepare your food label.

If the food is tea or coffee: There are naming rules for coffee and tea. Please read the Food Standards Code to ensure your label is correct.

Coffee and tea include types that are:

  • caffeinated,
  • decaffeinated,
  • instant or
  • soluble

If your food is spring water or mineral water: Spring and mineral water means ground water.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.6.1 Fruit juice and vegetable juice
  • Standard 2.6.2 Non-alcoholic beverages and brewed soft drinks
  • Standard 2.10.4 Miscellaneous standards for other foods

sections.title: Nuts and seeds
sections.content:
Food that is sold as peanut butter must be a peanut based spread that has no less than 850 g/kg of peanuts.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.10.4 Miscellaneous standards for other foods

sections.title: Oils and margarine
sections.content:
Margarine means an edible oil spread containing no less than 800 g/kg of edible oils.

You can only name your food an oil spread or table margarine, if the food contain no less than 55 μg/kg of vitamin D.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.4.2 Edible oil spreads

sections.title: Salt and salt products
sections.content:
Foods that are labelled salt or a salt product have special requirements. These products cannot make nutrition or health claim, must have extra information in the nutrition information panel and must be made from certain elements.

You need to read the Food Standards Code to ensure your label is correct.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.10.2 Salt and salt products
  • Standard 2.10.4 Miscellaneous standards for other foods

sections.title: Sugar and sugar alternatives
sections.content:
Food that is sold as white sugar or a sugar must be purified crystallised sucrose and have no less than 99.7% sucrose when dry.

Food that is sold as icing must be a mixture of sugar and other foods for use as a coating and includes frosting, plastic icing and icing gel.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.8.1 Sugar and sugar products

sections.title: Vinegar
sections.content:
A food that is sold as imitation vinegar or vinegar must contain no less than 40 g/kg of acetic acid.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.10.1 Vinegar and related products

content.description: Food labels must include the business details (name and address) of the supplier on the label. A supplier is a business which packs, manufactures, sells or imports food. Business details help consumers, other businesses and government agencies know who to contact in the event of a complaint or food recall.

questions.label: Business name
questions.hint: This is the name of the food business that is the supplier, manufacturer, packer, vendor or importer of the food.

questions.label: Business address
questions.hint: A business address is the street address, or a description of the location, of the premises, where the business is operating in Australia. A post office box or similar is not allowed.

sections.title: Business details
sections.content:
Business details are the name and address of the food business that is the supplier, manufacturer, packer, vendor or importer of the food.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirements to have labels or otherwise provide information
  • Standard 1.2.2 Information requirements – food identification

Food Standards Australia and New Zealand

  • User Guides - Overview of Food Labelling

sections.title: Food sold from a vending machine
sections.content:
If your food is sold from a vending machine:
The name and business address of the supplier of the vending machine must be clearly displayed on the vending machine.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirements to have labels or otherwise provide information

sections.title: Food sold in a hamper
sections.content:
If your food is sold in a hamper (e.g. gourmet cheese, olives and nuts in a gift box with cheese knife):
The name and address of the supplier of the hamper must be provided with the hamper.

Note: Labelling information must be provided for each item of food in the hamper. This can include information on a label for packaged food, or information provided in a product sheet for unpackaged food.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirements to have labels or otherwise provide information

sections.title: Kava and kava root
sections.content:
If the food for sale is not in a package and consists of kava root:
The name and address for the supplier of the kava root must

  • Be displayed with the food; or
  • Accompany the food for sale

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirements to have labels or otherwise provide information

content.heading: No date mark is required
content.content:
No date marking information is required for a food with a shelf life of more than 2 years.

If date marking is not required, a food business must add a lot identification so that the food can be identified.

content.heading: Best-before, baked-on or baked-for date
content.content:
Bread with a shelf life of less than 7 days can be labelled using either a:

  • Best-before date
  • Baked-for date
  • Baked-on date

content.heading: Use-by date
content.content: These foods must be labelled with a use-by date because they may become unsafe to eat after the use-by date has passed. A food may look, smell and taste ok but be unsafe to eat.

content.heading: Best-before date
content.content: A best-before date is required for all foods with a shelf life of 2 years or less that do not need a use-by date. The best-before date is the date up to which the food remains with good appearance, smell and taste, and keeps any qualities for which a claim has been made.

sections.title: What is a date mark?
sections.content:
A date mark is a guide to how long a food will last. All packaged food with a shelf life of two years or less must show a date mark, except for individual portions of ice cream or ice confection.

Shelf life refers to the length of time a food remains:

  • safe to eat
  • looks, smells and tastes ok, and
  • retains any specific qualities for which claims have been made.

A use-by date is required when a food becomes unsafe to eat. Food cannot be sold and should not be eaten after its use-by date. A food can be eaten past its best-before date, but may not look, smell or taste the same as when it was fresh. Bread with a shelf life of less than 7 days, can be date marked with a baked-on or baked-for date.

It may be necessary to seek expert advice from a food testing laboratory:

  • to determine your food’s shelf life
  • to determine what type of date mark is required for your food.

The Food Standards Code gives rules for the format of the date mark (how it appears on label). The day and month are required for a food with a shelf life of 3 months or less, whereas the month and year are required for a food with a longer shelf life.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.5 Information requirements – date marking of food for sale

sections.title: Baked-on and baked-for dates
sections.content:
The label on a package of bread with a shelf life of less than 7 days may be date marked with a baked-on date or a baked-for date instead of a best-before date.

The baked-on date means the date on which the bread was baked.

The baked-for date means:

  • If the time at which the bread was baked is before midday – the baked-on date
  • If the time at which the bread was baked is after midday – the day after the baked-on date. Bread that is baked after midday on one day may have a baked-for date of the following day. The baked-for date must not be later than 12 hours after the time the bread was baked.

The words ‘Baked On’ or ‘Baked For’, or the shortened terms, ‘Bkd On’ or ‘Bkd For’, must be included on the label followed by the date, for example, Bkd On 15 Apr.

Further reading

Queensland Health publication

  • Bread and Bakery Products

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.5 Information requirements – date marking of food for sale

sections.title: Best-before dates
sections.content:
A best-before date is the last date on which you can expect a food to look, smell and taste fresh, and to keep any property for which a claim has been made. This is on the condition that the food has been stored according to any storage conditions on the label and the package is unopened.

A food that has passed its best-before date will still be safe to eat.

The words ‘Best Before’ must be included on the label followed by the date, or a direction provided about where the date is located. For example:

  • Best Before 23 Dec 2021
  • Best Before – see base of can

Foods may be sold after the best-before date if the food has not spoiled and complies with any other applicable legislation.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.5 Information requirements – date marking of food for sale

sections.title: Date mark formats
sections.content:
The day, month and year must be written so that it is clear which number refers to the day, the month or the year.

The month can be expressed in either:

  • numerical form, e.g. 01 for January; or
  • in letters, which can be upper case, e.g. JAN or JANUARY, or lower case, e.g. Jan or January.

The year can be expressed in numerical form using either:

  • 2 digits, e.g. 21; or
  • 4 digits, e.g. 2021.

The date format depends on the shelf life of the food. The day and month (e.g. 15/03/2020) are required for a food with a shelf life of 3 months or less. The month and year (e.g.: Apr 2021) are required for a food with a longer shelf life.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.5 Information requirements – date marking of food for sale

sections.title: Lot identification
sections.content:
Lot identification means a number or other information that identifies the premises where the food was prepared or packed, and the batch the food is part of. This may be useful when several batches of the same food are prepared, manufactured or packed on the same day. There is no set format for lot identification.

It is not always necessary to include a lot identification on a label if a date mark, business name and address can identify the food. If date marking is not required, lot identification must be added so that the food can be identified.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.2 Information requirements – food identification

sections.title: Use-by dates
sections.content:
The use-by date is the date after which the food should not be eaten because it is no longer safe, provided it has been stored according to any stated storage conditions on the label and the package is unopened.

For example, milk is usually labelled with a use-by date because it may become unsafe before it becomes rancid, bitter, or separates.

You will need to determine the shelf life of your food to work out how long it can be safely stored. It is recommended you seek professional advice from a food testing laboratory.

The words ‘Use By’ must be included on the label followed by the date. For example, Use By 23 Dec 2021.

Food cannot be sold and should not be eaten after the use-by date.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.5 Information requirements – date marking of food for sale

sections.title: Food in small packages
sections.content:
If the food is sold in a small package where the package has a surface area of less than 100 cm2 only a use-by date needs to be included. For example: A small bar of chocolate.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.5 Information requirements – date marking of food for sale

sections.title: Ice cream or ice confection
sections.content:
If the food is a single serve of ice cream or ice confection no date marking information is required.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.5 Information requirements – date marking of food for sale

sections.title: Directions for use
sections.content:
Directions for use are instructions for how to prepare the food so that it is ready to eat. This includes directions required for health or safety reasons.

For example: frozen chicken tenders may have the directions for use as ‘This is a raw product. Must be cooked prior to eating. Cook from frozen. Please ensure chicken is fully cooked before eating’.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.6 Information requirements – directions for use and storage

sections.title: Storage conditions
sections.content:
Storage conditions are instructions about how to store food so that the food will keep until the best-before or use-by date.

For example, storage conditions for milk may be ‘store below 5°C’.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.6 Information requirements – directions for use and storage

sections.title: Bamboo shoots
sections.content:
If the food is raw bamboo shoots:
The label must include directions for use indicating that bamboo shoots should be fully cooked before being eaten.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.6 Information requirements – directions for use and storage

sections.title: Cassava
sections.content:
If the food is raw sweet cassava:
The label must include directions for use indicating that sweet cassava should be peeled and fully cooked before being consumed.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.6 Information requirements – directions for use and storage

sections.title: Fish, crustacea and seafood
sections.content:
If the food is raw fish which has been moulded or combined to look like a cut or fillet of fish:
The label must say that the food is either formed or joined and give cooking instructions to make it safe to eat.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.6 Information requirements – directions for use and storage
  • Standard 2.2.3 Fish and fish products.
    • See section 2.2.3—3 Labelling of formed or joined fish

sections.title: Meat and meat products
sections.content:
If the food is raw meat which has been moulded or combined to look like a cut of meat:
The label must say that the food is either formed or joined and give cooking instructions to make it safe to eat.

Further reading

  • Standard 1.2.6 Information requirements – directions for use and storage
  • Standard 2.2.1 Meat and meat products.
    • See section 2.2.1—8 Information about raw meat joined or formed into the semblance of a cut of meat

sections.title: What is an ingredient list?
sections.content:
The ingredient list is a statement of ingredients that are used to make the food. The ingredient list must be shown on the label for most packaged food.

Some packaged foods do not need an ingredient list. For example:

  • Individual portion packs
  • Foods in small packages
  • Foods with one ingredient
  • Water that is packaged and labelled in accordance with Standard 2.6.2 of the Food Standards Code. See non-alcoholic drinks in food with extra requirements for more information.
  • Whole or cut fruit and vegetables in packaging that does not obscure its nature or quality.

An ingredient is to be listed using either:

  • the common name
  • a name that describes the true nature of the ingredient
  • a generic name specified in the Food Standards Code.
  • a required name if the ingredient is, or contains, an allergen

The ingredient name may also need a further description to ensure that the consumer is not misled about the nature of an ingredient. For example: if cheese powder is used as an ingredient, it should be listed as “cheese powder” instead of “cheese”.

Ingredients that contain allergens must be identified in the ingredient list using a required name. Allergens include: cereals such as barley, oats and rye that contain gluten, wheat, milk, egg, peanuts, tree nuts (i.e.: almond, Brazil nut, cashew, hazelnut, macadamia, pecan, pine nut, pistachio, walnut), fish, crustacea, mollusc, sesame seed, soybeans, lupin and sulphites.

There are requirements in the Food Standards Code for how ingredients are listed. You must:

  • List ingredients in descending order of ingoing weight
  • Declare all of the ingredients that make up a compound ingredient, if it contributes 5% or more to the final food.
  • Declare food additives including flavouring substances
  • Define the percentage of a characterising ingredient and component in the food.
  • Declare where alternative ingredients are sometimes used to make the food.
  • Declare allergens using the required names and format the required name in bold text.

Some ingredients are exempt ingredients that do not need to be included in the ingredient list.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirements to have labels or otherwise provide information
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients
  • Standard 1.2.10 Information requirements – characterising ingredients and components of food
  • Standard 1.3.3 Processing aids
  • Schedule 7 Food additive class names (for statement of ingredients)
  • Schedule 8 Food additive names and code numbers (for statement of ingredients)
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations
  • Schedule 10 Generic names of ingredients and conditions for their use
  • Schedule 16 Types of substances that may be used as food additives

Food Standards Australia and New Zealand

  • User Guides - Overview of Food Labelling

sections.title: Alternative ingredients
sections.content:
Where from time to time, a food ingredient or additive is replaced with another food or additive that serves the same function, both can be listed, provided it is clear that a substitute or alternative ingredient is being declared.

For example, the statement of ingredients may read: safflower or sunflower oil.

sections.title: Characterising ingredients
sections.content:
If you mention an ingredient, category of ingredients or a part of the food in the name on the label, then it becomes a characterising ingredient or component.

If an ingredient is usually associated with the food (for example, fruit in Christmas pudding), or is emphasised on the label in words, pictures, or graphics) then it is a characterising ingredient.

For example:

  • Strawberries are a characterising ingredient in strawberry yogurt
  • Meat is a characterising ingredient in a meat pie
  • Honey is a characterising ingredient in a yoghurt with a picture of a pot of honey on the label

The amount of the characterising ingredients in the food must be written on the label as a percentage or, if declared in the nutrition information panel, as the average quantity per serving and per unit quantity. For example, strawberry yoghurt ingredients must state Strawberries (23%).

If the amount of the characterising ingredient is less than 5%, then the proportion must be given to the nearest 0.5 decimal place, e.g. Banana (4.5%)

The percentage information is not required for the following:

  • prepared filled rolls, sandwiches, bagels or similar products
  • food sold at a fundraising event, for example, cake stalls and school fetes
  • food sold in small packages
  • cured and/or dried meat flesh in whole cuts or pieces
  • foods with one ingredient
  • ingredient or category of ingredients that is used in small quantities for the purpose of flavouring, for example, herb and garlic bread

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.1.2 Definitions used throughout the Code
    • See section 1.1.2—4 Definition of characterising component and characterising ingredient
  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirements to have labels or otherwise provide information
    • See section 1.2.1—9 Information requirements for food for sale that is not required to bear a label
  • Standard 1.2.10 Information requirements – characterising ingredients and components of food.

Food Standards Australia New Zealand

  • User Guide – Percentage labelling of food

sections.title: Compound ingredients
sections.content:
A compound ingredient is an ingredient that contains two or more ingredients.

For example:

  • Tomato paste is an ingredient in a pre-made pizza base. The tomato paste is a compound ingredient as it is made up of the following ingredients: tomato, canola oil, olive oil, sugar, salt, citric acid (330), basil, oregano.
  • Dark chocolate chips are used as an ingredient in chocolate chip muffins. The dark chocolate chips are a compound ingredient as they are made up of the following ingredients: sugar, cocoa mass, cocoa butter, natural vanilla flavour.

If a food contains compound ingredients which contributes 5% or more to the final food, then all the foods and additives in that compound ingredient must be declared in the ingredient list.

If a food contains compound ingredients which contribute less than 5% to the final food, then only allergens and food additives must be listed.

sections.title: Exempt ingredients
sections.content:
The ingredient list does not need to include:

  • An ingredient which is completely removed during processing. For example: through evaporation.
  • Added water that:
    • is added to reconstitute dehydrated or concentrated ingredients; or
    • forms part of broth, brine or syrup that is declared in the statement of ingredients or is part of the name of the food; or
    • constitutes less than 5% of the food; or
  • A food or substance that is used as a processing aid – except in some circumstances (refer to processing aids section).
  • An ingredient of a flavouring substance (additive) – except in some circumstances (refer to food additives section)

The ingoing weight of water or an ingredient which is completely removed during processing must be calculated according to Standard 1.2.4—5 of the Food Standards Code and added to the statement of ingredients in the order of descending weight.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirements to have labels or otherwise provide information
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients
  • Standard 1.3.3 Processing aids

sections.title: Food additives and flavours
sections.content:
If you are adding food additives:
Food additives are substances added to foods to keep them fresh or to enhance their colour, flavour or texture. They may include food colourings, flavour enhancers (such as MSG) or a range of preservatives. Most food additives are listed on the product label, along with other ingredients, in descending order by weight (flavours are an exception and do not need to be identified).

In most cases you can define the food additive with either its name or the code number. Refer to schedule 7 and schedule 8 for food additive class names and code numbers.
For example, cochineal may be listed as colour (cochineal) or colour (120).

If the food additive or flavouring contains allergens:
The allergen must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name. For example: caramel can be listed as caramel [150a milk]. Monosodium L-glutamate (MSG) can be listed MSG (wheat).

If you are adding vitamins and minerals:
Vitamins and minerals are a specific type of food additive. The vitamin or mineral may be declared using the class name of ‘vitamin’ or ‘mineral’.
Claims may be made about the presence of vitamins or minerals in food. However, there are complex labelling requirements for making these claims that are not covered by Label Buster.
It is recommended that you seek professional advice from a food labelling consultant to prepare your food label.

If the food is, or contains sulphites:
Sulphites must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name of ‘sulphites’ when added sulphites are in concentrations of 10mg/kg or more.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.1.2 Definitions used throughout the Code
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
    • see 1.2.3 Division 3 Mandatory declarations
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients
    • See section 1.2.4—7 Declaration of substances used as food additives
    • See section 1.2.4—8 Declaration of vitamins and minerals
  • Standard 1.2.10 Information requirements – characterising ingredients and components of food.
  • Standard 1.3.1 Food additives
  • Schedule 7 Food additive class names (for statement of ingredients)
  • Schedule 8 Food additive names and code numbers (for statement of ingredients)
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations
  • Schedule 16 Types of substances that may be used as food additives
  • Schedule 17 Vitamins and minerals

sections.title: Generic names
sections.content:
Generic names may be used in the ingredient list, instead of:

  • a common name of an ingredient, or
  • a name that describes the true nature of the ingredient.

The following generic names of foods can be used without any specific conditions:

  • cereals
  • cheese
  • cocoa butter
  • crystallised fruit
  • fruit
  • gum bases
  • herbs
  • meat
  • milk protein
  • poultry meat
  • spices
  • vegetables

For example, the term ‘fruit’ can be used in place of bananas or oranges.

The following generic food names may only be used under specific conditions in the Food Standards Code:

  • fats or oils
  • fish
  • offal
  • starch
  • sugar

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—4 Ingredients to be listed by common, descriptive or generic name
  • Schedule 10 Generic names of ingredients and conditions for their use

sections.title: Order of ingredients
sections.content:
All ingredients must be listed in descending order of ingoing weight. This means that the ingredient with the greatest amount is listed first, then the ingredient with the second greatest amount and so on.

For food that is intended to be returned to its original state by the addition of water (reconstitued), the ingredients may be listed in descending order of their weight in the reconstitued food. In this instance, it must be made clear on the label.

Further reading

To calculate and show the ingoing weight for water and other ingredients that disappear when cooked, read:
Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—5 Ingredients to be listed in descending order of ingoing weight

sections.title: Processing aids
sections.content:
A processing aid is a food or substance that is used during manufacture. For example, an antifoaming or clarifying agent. A processing aid is often an exempt ingredient, which does not have to be included in the ingredient list.

However, if it contains an allergen, it must be included in the ingredient list using the words ‘processing aid’ followed by the required name of the allergen.

For example:

  • Processing aid (wheat)
  • Processing aid (wheat, egg)

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

Australian Standard Fish Names

  • A searchable database of Australian Standard Fish Names is available at http://www.fishnames.com.au
  • Hard copies of the Australian Fish Names Standard (AS 5300) are available from FRDC’s Online Shop at https://infostore.saiglobal.com/en-au/Standards/AS-5300-2019-111200_SAIG_AS_AS_2741382/

sections.title: Required names
sections.content:
Required names are to be used in the ingredient list and the separate summary statement to identify allergens in the food.

  • Fish, crustacea and molluscs must be separately declared in both the ingredient list and summary statement, using ‘fish’, ‘crustacean’ and ‘mollusc’ as required names.
  • The following tree nuts must be declared separately in the ingredient list and summary statement using the required name– ‘almond’, ‘Brazil nut’, ‘cashew’, ‘hazelnut’, ‘macadamia’, ‘pecan’, ‘pine nut’, ‘pistachio’, ‘walnut’.
  • ‘Wheat’ must be used as the required name in the ingredient list and summary statement when wheat (or its hybrids) is present. If gluten is present, then ‘gluten’ must also be included in the summary statement.
  • ‘Rye’, ‘barley’ and ‘oats’ (if they contain gluten) must be used as the required names in the ingredient list when these cereals (or their hybrids) are present. However, they must be declared as ‘gluten’ in the summary statement.
  • Soybean must be declared in the ingredient list as either ‘soy’, ‘soya’ or ‘soybean’ and in the summary statement as ‘soy’.
  • The required names for other allergens for use in the ingredient list and summary statement, are ‘sulphites’ (when added in concentrations of 10 mg/kg or more), ‘milk’, ‘egg’, ‘sesame’, ‘lupin’ and ‘peanut’.
  • The term ‘processing aid’ (or its plural) must be listed in the ingredient list in association with the allergen/s it contains or is derived from, e.g. processing aids (wheat, egg).

The required name must be the same font size as all other ingredient names and printed in bold font type.

The allergen may be present in the food as:

  • An ingredient
  • An ingredient of a compound ingredient
  • A substance used as a processing aid, or an ingredient or component of that substance.
  • A substance used as a food additive, or an ingredient or component of that substance.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

Australian Standard Fish Names

  • A searchable database of Australian Standard Fish Names is available at http://www.fishnames.com.au
  • Hard copies of the Australian Fish Names Standard (AS 5300) are available from FRDC’s Online Shop at https://infostore.saiglobal.com/en-au/Standards/AS-5300-2019-111200_SAIG_AS_AS_2741382/

sections.title: Breads, cereals and grains
sections.content:
If the ingredient is a cereal that is barley, oats, rye or a hybridised strain of barley, oats, rye:
The name of the cereal ingredient must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name ‘barley’, ‘oats’, ‘rye’ when:

  • the cereal or its hybridised strain contains gluten and the cereal is used to make foods other than beer or spirits e.g. Oats are used as an ingredient to make a muesli bar. The ingredients list for the muesli bar is described as – oats, coconut, sultanas, sugar, honey, cinnamon.

If the ingredient is a cereal that is wheat or a hybridised strain of wheat:
The name of the cereal ingredient must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name ‘wheat’, other than when it is found in:

  • beer or spirits
  • alcohol distilled from wheat
  • glucose syrups that are made from wheat starch and that:
    • have been subject to a refining process that has removed gluten protein content to the lowest level that is reasonably achievable, not exceeding 20mg/kg.
    e.g. 1. If spelt is an ingredient, the required name ‘wheat’ must be used in the ingredient list i.e. spelt (wheat) 2. If triticale (a wheat rye hybrid) is an ingredient, the required names ‘wheat’ and ‘rye’ must be used in the ingredient list as – triticale (wheat, rye).

If the ingredient is starch:
The generic name of ‘starch’ may be used to describe an ingredient for any unmodified starch or any starch which has been modified by other means or enzymes.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—4 Ingredients to be listed by common, descriptive or generic name
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations
  • Schedule 10 Generic names of ingredients and conditions for their use

sections.title: Eggs and egg products
sections.content:
If the food is, or contains eggs:
Egg must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name of 'egg' or 'eggs'. For example: The ingredients list for egg noodles is described as -- Wheat flour, water, eggs, salt.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
    • See 1.2.3 Division 3 Mandatory declarations
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

sections.title: Fish, crustacea and seafood
sections.content:
If the food is, or contains crustacea:
The name of the crustacea, followed by the required name ‘crustacean’ must be declared in the ingredient list.
e.g. crab (crustacean), crayfish (crustacean).

If the food is, or contains fish:
The name of the crustacea, followed by the required name ‘fish’ must be declared in the ingredient list.
e.g. barramundi (fish), hake (fish).

If the food is, or contains molluscs:
The name of the mollusc, followed by the required name ‘mollusc’ must be declared in the ingredient list.
e.g. oyster (mollusc), squid (mollusc).

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
    • See section 1.2.3—4 Mandatory declaration of certain foods or substances in food
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations
  • Schedule 10 Generic names of ingredients and conditions for their use

Australian Standard Fish Names

  • A searchable database of Australian Standard Fish Names is available at http://www.fishnames.com.au
  • Hard copies of the Australian Fish Names Standard (AS 5300) are available from FRDC’s Online Shop at https://infostore.saiglobal.com/en-au/Standards/AS-5300-2019-111200_SAIG_AS_AS_2741382/

sections.title: Fruit and vegetables
sections.content:
If the food is a juice blend:
The name and percentage of the of the juice in the blend must be included in the ingredients. For example: Tropical juice (Pineapple 50%, mango 20%, oranges 10%, apple 10%, passionfruit 5%, peach puree 5%)

If the food is an orange juice blend:
Where an orange juice blend has less than 10% in total of:

  • mandarin juice; or
  • tangelo juice; or
  • mandarin and tangelo juice
the orange juice is not required to be labelled as a juice blend.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.6.1 Fruit juice and vegetable juice

sections.title: Legumes and pulses
sections.content:
If the food is, or contains soy
Soy must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name of either 'soy', 'soya', or 'soybean', except for:

  • soybean oil that has been degummed, neutralised, bleached and deodorised
  • soybean derivatives that are tocopherol or phytosterol

If the food is, or contains lupin:
Lupin must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name of 'lupin'.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements -- warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
    • See 1.2.3 Division 3 mandatory declarations
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

sections.title: Meat and meat products
sections.content:
If the food is minced meat: the maximum proportion of fat in the mince must be provided.

If the food contains offal:
Offal includes blood, brain, heart, kidney, liver, pancreas, spleen, thymus, tongue and tripe, and excludes meat flesh, bone and bone marrow.

For brain, heart, kidney, liver, tongue or tripe, the food name or description must be identified as either:

  • offal
  • the specific name of the type of offal

For any other type of offal, the food name or description must be identified by the specific name of the type of offal.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—4 Ingredients to be listed by common, descriptive or generic name
  • Standard 2.2.1 Meat and meat products.
    • See section 2.2.1—6 Statement indicating the presence of offal
    • See section 2.2.1—7 Proportion of fat in minced meat

sections.title: Milk, dairy and dairy substitutes
sections.content:
Milk or food or ingredients containing milk must be identified in the ingredient list using the required name ‘milk’ (except when the food is alcohol distilled from whey).

If the ingredient name contains the word ‘milk’ as a separate word, it meets the required name requirements, but the required name must be in bold type e.g. milk solids, milk protein.

The required name must be a separate word. For example, buttermilk must be listed in the ingredient list as buttermilk (milk).

If the ingredient name does not include the required name, then the required name must be provided with the ingredient name. For example: cheese (milk).

The generic name of ‘milk solid’ may be used to describe an ingredient that is:

  • Milk powder, skim milk powder or dried milk products; or
  • Any 2 or more of the following ingredients:
    • whey
    • whey powder
    • whey proteins
    • lactose
    • caseinates
    • milk proteins
    • milk fat.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—4 Ingredients to be listed by common, descriptive or generic name
  • Schedule 10 Generic names of ingredients and conditions for their use

sections.title: Non-alcoholic drinks
sections.content:
If the food is packaged water:
The ingredients list is not required for a water that is packaged and labelled to the requirements of Standard 2.6.2.

If the food is a juice blend:
The name and percentage of the of the juice in the blend must be included in the ingredients. For example: Tropical juice (Pineapple 50%, mango 20%, oranges 10%, apple 10%, passionfruit 5%, peach puree 5%)

If the food is an orange juice blend:
Where an orange juice blend has less than 10% in total of:

  • mandarin juice; or
  • tangelo juice; or
  • mandarin and tangelo juice
the orange juice is not required to be labelled as a juice blend

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—2 Requirement for statement of ingredients
  • Standard 2.6.1 Fruit juice and vegetable juice
  • Standard 2.6.2 Non-alcoholic beverages and brewed soft drinks

sections.title: Nuts and seeds
sections.content:
If the food is, or contains nuts:
The name of the nut must be declared in the ingredient list using the required name for the nut:

  • almond
  • Brazil nut
  • cashew
  • hazelnut
  • macadamia
  • peanut
  • pecan
  • pine nut
  • pistachio
  • walnut.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
    • see 1.2.3 Division 3 Mandatory declarations
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

sections.title: Oils and margarine
sections.content:
If using the generic name of fats or oils:
The ingredient list must declare:

  • whether the source is animal or vegetable
  • if the food is a dairy product, including ice cream – the specific source of animal fats or oils.

The generic name must not be used for diacylglycerol oil.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 2.4.2 Edible oil spreads
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients
    • see section 1.2.4 Ingredients to be listed by common, descriptive or generic name.
  • Schedule 10 Generic names of ingredients and conditions for their use

sections.title: Sugar and sugar alternatives
sections.content:
If the food is, or contains sugar:
The name “sugars” must not be used in the ingredient list.

The generic name of sugar may be used to describe an ingredient that is:

  • white sugar
  • white refined sugar
  • caster sugar or castor sugar
  • loaf sugar or cube sugar
  • icing sugar
  • coffee sugar
  • coffee crystals
  • raw sugar

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—4 Ingredients to be listed by common, descriptive or generic name
  • Schedule 10 Generic names of ingredients and conditions for their use

sections.title: Food in small packages
sections.content:
If the food sold in a small package where the package has a surface area of less than 100 cm2:
The ingredient list is not required is not required for food in small packages.
For example: A small a packet of chewing gum or a small bar of chocolate.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—2 Requirement for statement of ingredients

sections.title: Food with one ingredient
sections.content:
If the food has only one ingredient:
the ingredient list is not required.
For example: A bag of rice, frozen corn kernels, apple juice.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.4 Information requirements – statement of ingredients.
    • See section 1.2.4—2 Requirement for statement of ingredients

sections.title: Advisory statements
sections.content:
Advisory statements let consumers know important information about the safety (e.g. unpasteurised), suitability (e.g. not suitable as a complete milk replacement for children under 5 years) and effect (e.g. laxative) of the food or ingredient.

An advisory statement must provide the same meaning as the statement listed in the Food Standards Code but can be written in your own words.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

Food Standards Australia and New Zealand

  • User Guide – Warning and Advisory Statements and Declarations

sections.title: Allergen declarations
sections.content:
Some foods and ingredients can cause allergic reactions and must be stated on the label.

You must state any allergen listed in Standard 1.2.3 when present in a food as:

  • An ingredient
  • An ingredient of a compound ingredient
  • A substance used as a food additive
  • An ingredient or component of a food additive
  • A substance or food used as a processing aid
  • An ingredient or component of a processing aid.

The presence of an allergen in a food must be included in the ingredient list and in a summary statement using the required names. The summary statement must be:

  • separate from the ingredient list
  • located near the ingredient list
  • printed in bold font
  • use the same typeface and size as the ingredient list
  • start with the word ‘Contains’
  • must not include any other words except for the required names that can be used for the summary statement.

Note: Sometimes a different required name must be used in the ingredient list and summary statement.

Allergen declarations are required on individual portion packs that have a surface area of 30cm2 or greater.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code

  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirement to have labels or otherwise provide information
    • See section 1.2.1—6 When the food for sale must bear a label
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations.
    • See 1.2.3 Division 3 Mandatory declarations
  • Schedule 9 Mandatory advisory statements and declarations

Allergen Bureau - the peak industry body representing food industry allergen management in Australia and New Zealand.

  • https://allergenbureau.net/

sections.title: Warning statements
sections.content:
The warning statement must be displayed on the label in the exact words and type size as specified in the Food Standards Code. Warning statements must be a minimum size of type of 3 mm. In the case of small packages, a minimum size of type of 1.5 mm is required.
Warning statement are required on individual portions packs that have a surface area of 30cm2 or greater.

Further reading

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code
  • Standard 1.2.1 Requirement to have labels or otherwise provide information
    • See section 1.2.1—6 When the food for sale must bear a label
  • Standard 1.2.3 Information requirements – warning statements, advisory statements and declarations
  • Standard 2.6.3 Kava

Food Standards Australia and New Zealand

  • User Guide – Warning and Advisory Statements and Declarations

content.heading: Congratulations! You have completed all the steps in Label Buster.
content.content: Using your responses to each question, Label Buster has generated a product sheet and an example food label.
Don’t forget to refer to the Allergen labelling fact sheet to make the changes required to ensure that your label is fully compliant with the Food Standards Code requirements.

If you have trouble or have any further questions in relation to incorporating the allergen requirements into your label, please contact the Food Safety Standards and Regulation Unit via foodsafety@health.qld.gov.au or phone (07) 3328 9310.
